data.hypothesis: The five measured programs are distinct, with no repeated source; valid 2-, 3-, 4-, and 8-output candidates cluster between 3.3866 and 3.4491 µs, while 16 outputs measured 4.9264 µs. These close small-chunk results do not establish a chunk-size cause, so test six outputs as a contrast: four Y groups per block cover 24 rows, halving Y-block count versus the prior three-output layout while keeping the same nine-scalar rolling window. Reduced scheduling overhead may help this small workload, but longer per-thread work may hurt; no speedup is assumed.

memory_lessons.applicability: These measurements are for the supplied fixed workload and do not establish a general chunk-size optimum or causal speedup.
memory_lessons.claim: The measured 2-, 3-, 4-, and 8-output candidates were close in mean time (about 3.39–3.45 µs); the 16-output candidate was slower at about 4.93 µs. All reported candidates passed the supplied correctness cases.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Have the controller run correctness and repeated official timings for the six-output candidate against the baseline and prior candidates; only draw conclusions after compatible measurements.

Controller validation and official timing are still required.
transformations: Replace the shared-memory derivative with one kernel and one launch; use blocks of 32 adjacent-X lanes by four Y groups.
Give each thread up to six consecutive Y outputs using a nine-scalar register window, shifting it and loading one entering row between valid outputs.
Apply the specified boundary adjustment to each sampled coordinate: add 63 below zero, subtract 63 above 63, and leave 0–63 unchanged; guard final partial Y groups and outputs.
